extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of corporate social responsibility (CSR), business policy makers and researchers
extracted.subtask_description: An encyclopedic overview of corporate social responsibility (CSR) covering definitions, regional policies (notably EU/OECD), performance dimensions, reporting frameworks, supply-chain and reputation metrics, and examples of crisis-driven CSR. Useful as a reference for students, managers, and policy makers designing or evaluating CSR activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: CSR (EU 2001 definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: “a concept whereby companies integrate social and environmental concerns in their business operations and in their interaction with their stakeholders on a voluntary basis.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the European Commission's early definition (2001) emphasizing voluntary integration of social/environmental concerns. The page contrasts this with later EU language that treats CSR more strategically and less purely voluntary.

rubrics_metrics.name: CSR (EU 2011 strategic definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: “the responsibility of enterprises for their impact on society.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 2011 EU revision frames CSR as a responsibility tied to enterprise impacts and endorses a 'strategic approach' linking CSR to competitiveness. The Commission also stated enterprises should have processes to integrate social, environmental, ethical, human rights and consumer concerns into business operations and core strategy in close collaboration with stakeholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: EU CSR Strategy objectives (2011–2014)
rubrics_metrics.description: Actions planned under the 2011–2014 agenda were aimed at: enhancing visibility of CSR and disseminating good practices; improving and tracking levels of trust in business; improving self- and co-regulation processes; enhancing market reward for CSR; improving company disclosure of social and environmental information; further integrating CSR into education, training, and research; emphasising the importance of national and sub-national CSR policies; better aligning European and global approaches to CSR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These enumerated objectives function as evaluation/implementation priorities for EU-focused CSR policy and can be used as a checklist when assessing whether an enterprise's CSR strategy aligns with EU aims (visibility, disclosure, education, policy alignment, trust-building, market incentives, regulatory approaches).

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsible Business Conduct / integration process (OECD)
rubrics_metrics.description: Enterprises should have in place a process to integrate social, environmental, ethical, human rights and consumer concerns into their business operations and core strategy in close collaboration with their stakeholders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This echoes the OECD's 'responsible business conduct' framing and the OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises; it implies an operational requirement (a process) rather than ad-hoc actions, and emphasizes stakeholder collaboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three CSR performance areas (human, product, environmental responsibility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment areas: human responsibility, product responsibility, and environmental responsibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anselmsson and Johansson's descriptions: human responsibility — dealing with suppliers who adhere to good animal breeding/farming principles and maintaining fair/positive working conditions for employees; product responsibility — products come with a complete list of content, country of origin is stated, upholding declarations of intent and assuming liability; environmental responsibility — company perceived to produce environmentally-friendly, ecological, and non-harmful products. Use these as distinct dimensions when evaluating retailer CSR performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reputation / CSR perception metrics (Reputation Institute / RepTrak)
rubrics_metrics.description: RI monitors social responsibility reputations by focusing on the perception of consumers regarding company governance, positive impact on the community and society, and treatment of the workforce; it rates each criterion with the firm's proprietary RepTrak Pulse platform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reputation-based scoring emphasizes perceptions (governance, community impact, workforce treatment). Useful when assessing CSR through consumer-facing reputation indices rather than only internal compliance or disclosure metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Company disclosure and transparency
rubrics_metrics.description: Improving company disclosure of social and environmental information (explicit EU objective).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page references multiple reporting resources and guidance (UN Global Compact, UNCTAD guidance on corporate responsibility indicators, UNCTAD guidance on governance disclosure, ISO 26000, GoodCorporation Standard). Disclosure is both a policy objective and an evaluative criterion — transparency of social/environmental information is expected and often benchmarked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social license to operate
rubrics_metrics.description: The concept that businesses must obtain legitimacy from communities and stakeholders — 'social licence to operate' — achieved and maintained through relationships, trust, and acceptable company responses to community protest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Literature cited offers principles for achieving/maintaining social licence; criteria include meaningful stakeholder relationships, responsiveness to protests, community engagement, and legitimacy-building activities. Use qualitative community acceptance as an evaluative dimension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Crisis response, remediation and learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Crises have encouraged adoption of CSR (examples: Exxon Valdez, Mattel lead paint recall, Magellan Metals contamination, Odwalla E. coli outbreak leading to recalls and introduction of 'flash pasteurization' and open communication).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative criteria include speed and scope of recalls/cleanups, adoption of new risk-management/quality-control processes, openness of communication with customers/stakeholders, and demonstrable organizational learning (e.g., process change like flash pasteurization).

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsible supply chain management
rubrics_metrics.description: CSR applied to supplier relationships and procurement: socially responsible purchasing, supply-chain auditing, and ensuring suppliers adhere to labour/ethical/environmental standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: References include research on socially responsible supply chains, auditing in supply networks, SRP (socially responsible purchasing), verification resources (GSA Sustainable Facilities Tool, resources for verifying sustainable products), and initiatives like the Ethical Trading Initiative. Criteria: supplier compliance, audit systems, traceability, verification, and sustainable sourcing strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stakeholder engagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Stakeholders include customers, employees, shareholders, society, natural environment, business associates, regulatory agencies, future generations, etc.; CSR requires interaction with and consideration of these stakeholders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective CSR requires identification, engagement and collaboration with relevant stakeholders. Evaluation should consider whether stakeholder views are solicited, incorporated into strategy, and whether engagement is ongoing and substantive (not tokenistic).

rubrics_metrics.name: Context sensitivity / national and regional approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: Corporations that employ CSR behaviors do not always behave consistently in all parts of the world; a single behavior may not be considered ethical in all jurisdictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessments should account for local legal, cultural and normative differences; what counts as responsible conduct may vary by jurisdiction, so CSR policies often must be adapted while aiming for consistent principles where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adherence to international standards and frameworks
rubrics_metrics.description: References and guidance include: United Nations Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights (2011), OECD Guidelines for Multinational Enterprises (2011), ISO 26000, UN Global Compact, UNCTAD guidance on corporate responsibility indicators and governance disclosure, GoodCorporation Standard.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these frameworks as benchmarking tools for policies, due diligence, reporting and human rights/responsibility practices. Evaluations often check alignment with, or reporting against, these standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Triple bottom line (people, planet, profit)
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'triple bottom line' idea (People, Planet, Profit) as an evaluative lens for CSR and sustainability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess organizational performance across social, environmental and economic outcomes rather than purely financial metrics. The page notes historical discussion and critiques of the concept; it is commonly used to structure CSR objectives and reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: CSR as risk management
rubrics_metrics.description: Corporate Social Responsibility can function as a model for risk management in multinationals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether CSR activities are integrated into enterprise risk frameworks (identifying social/environmental risks, mitigation plans, and reputational protection). The literature cited frames CSR both as ethical practice and a strategic risk-management tool.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate CSR pillars/themes (practical company commitments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practical corporate CSR headings used by retailers (examples): Tesco — 'Trading responsibility', 'Reducing our Impact on the Environment', 'Being a Great Employer', 'Supporting Local Communities'; Sainsbury — 'Best for food and health', 'Sourcing with integrity', 'Respect for our environment', 'Making a difference to our community', 'A great place to work'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating corporate CSR programs, look for clear pillars/themes that map to environment, social welfare, ethical trading, and workplace quality; these make commitments measurable and communicable to stakeholders.
